newsitem.title: USA: JOBS-U.S. creates jobs, but not without some pain.
newsitem.headline: JOBS-U.S. creates jobs, but not without some pain.

text.p: By Rich Miller, Economics Correspondent
When it comes to creating jobs, the U.S. economy has been the envy of the rest of the industrial world in recent years.

But economists cautioned that those gains have not come without some pain and questioned how far countries in Europe and elsewhere can -- and should -- go in trying to emulate the success of America's free-wheeling jobs market.
"We've paid a price," Harvard University professor Richard Freeman said. "We've had one of the largest rises in income inequality since the great Depression."
In the last four years, U.S. employers have added more than 11-1/2 million new jobs to their payrolls -- far more than any other industrial nation.
The unemployment rate has fallen more or less steadily during that time and in January stood at 5.4 percent, around an eight-year low.

By contrast, European unemployment has soared to record levels and has shown scant sign of declining. In January, Germany's jobless rate was at a post-war high of 11.3 percent and that of France a record 12.7 percent.
Part of the disparity in the jobless rates can be explained by the different ways individual nations measure unemployment and by such special factors as the merger of east and west Germany.
For example, the Labour Department here puts west German unemployment at about 7.5 percent when measured on roughly the same basis as the United States.

But the figures for most other European countries do not look nearly as flattering. By the Labour Department's reckoning, unemployment in France is over 12 percent and Italy over 11 percent, even after the data are adjusted.

Cyclical factors also go some way toward explaining why the U.S. jobless rate looks so low when compared to Europe. The U.S. economic upswing is nearly six years old. Europe's expansion, by contrast, is still in its early stages.

But that begs the question of why Europe's economy has not recovered more. Some economists argue that interest rates in Europe are too high and budget policies too tight. The result: overvalued currencies, slow growth and high unemployment.

Most analysts though believe there is more at work in America's success in creating jobs than simple macroeconomic policies. Even at the height of its most recent economic expansion, Europe was unable to match America's jobs gains.
"They've had much less success in achieving lower unemployment rates than we have," Labour Department chief economist Edward Montgomery. US LABOUR MARKET MUCH MORE FLEXIBLE THAN EUROPE'S

The main reason, according to Montgomery and many other economists, is that the U.S. labour market is much more flexible than that of Europe's. There is far less government regulation in the United States, making it easier for American companies to hire -- and fire -- workers.
That is the case even though the United States has been adding to labour market legislation in recent years.

Edward Potter, President of the Employment Policy Foundation, said the United States has over 120 labour-related laws now, governing everything from occupational safety to the minimum wage. That compares with just 24 prior to 1960.
Unions too are far less powerful and pervasive in the United States than they are in Europe. Only about 15 percent of U.S. workers belong to a union, and many of them are in the public sector.

The flexibility of the U.S. labour market has allowed American employers to cut wages, rather than workers, when faced with technological change and stiff competition from low-cost producers in developing countries.

"We responded by letting wages fall to keep people employed," Princeton University professor and former Federal Reserve Vice Chair Alan Blinder said. "They (Europe) responded by holding up wages and letting people be unemployed."

The result is soaring joblessness in Europe and rising income inequality and worker insecurity in the United States, economists said. "We work many more hours than the Europeans," Harvard's Freeman said. "And our poor are poorer than the poor in Europe -- a lot poorer."
Some economists, such as John Schmitt of the Economic Policy Institute think tank, even argue it is better to be unemployed in Europe than to be a low-paid U.S. worker.

European governments provide their citizens with a whole host of benefits, including health care, that are not readily available in the United States. In contrast, Schmitt said, only about a quarter of America's lowest-paid workers receive health benefits from their companies.

In a forthcoming book, University of Southern California Assistant Professor David Finegold and Colin Crouch argue that what has set the United States apart has been the growth of women at work and part-time jobs for students and retirees.
"You can argue that the United States is divvying up the available work in more jobs," Finegold said.
The research also found that countries with strong Catholic societies tended to have lower jobs growth because fewer women are willing to leave the home and go to work.
"It's very hard to translate solutions (to the problem of unemployment) from one country to another," Finegold said.
